body.text: End of Solomon Islands-China security pact a 'holy grail' for Australia
It's about a 500-metre walk from the Solomon Islands government offices in Honiara to the Chinese embassy.
The big, nondescript grey building, with its intimidating fence and security system, looms ominously over the capital's main road, like an angry, oversized shipping container.

Early last month, the ABC has been told, a small delegation from the Solomon Islands government made the short journey there for a meeting to deliver some news, and they weren't going to hang around for some bubble tea and biscuits.
They were there to tell embassy staff that Solomon Islands would end its security pact with China.

There were rumours in the capital this week, which the ABC has been unable to confirm, that it was so secretive that all physical papers declaring the end of the security pact (which has a "non-disclosure clause") were promptly burnt to avoid any unwanted leaks.

Whether there's any truth to that is questionable, but either way it shows the sensitivity and impact of the decision — what one analyst this week described as Australia's "holy grail" in the Pacific.
Since it was announced suddenly in 2022, the China-Solomon Islands security pact has been the Zeitgeist for Australia and its Western allies' diplomatic assault in the Pacific.
Then in opposition, Foreign Minister Penny Wong called it Australia's "biggest foreign policy blunder since WWII".
The Albanese government has since gone about spending billions across the region, inking new treaties left, right and centre, including this week's $740 million agreement with Solomon Islands.

In Solomon Islands, the China security deal kicked off an almost farcical game of one-upmanship and gift-giving between the Australian government and the Chinese over the past four years, providing an infrastructure smorgasbord of stadiums, roads and buildings.
The Royal Solomon Islands Police Force was one of the main beneficiaries, with gifts sometimes delivered within days of each other.
Australia: You want some semiautomatic guns?
China: What about some awesome water cannons?
Australia: How about 60 cool new cars?
China: Drones are cooler than cars. We can throw in some actual human police as well!
It's led some political watchers to call the Royal Solomon Islands Police Force the most "over-resourced under-resourced" police force in the Asia-Pacific.
About a dozen or so Chinese police, called the "China Police Liaison Team", had been stationed permanently in the country, conducting training and what they called "community work".
Although their influence in Solomon Islands was often overblown, the presence of Chinese police officers in the country gave Canberra a lot of anxiety.
But the ABC understands the Chinese police will now leave the country, and very soon.

Solomon Islands academic Tarcisius Kabutaulaka told the ABC's Pacific Beat program he understood the Chinese police would leave at "the end of this month"; however, that has not been confirmed by either the Chinese or the Solomon Islands governments.
The other element that caused even more anxiety was the threat of a Chinese military base emerging in Solomon Islands.

Although it had been repeatedly ruled out by a succession of Solomon Islands' leaders — even the unpredictable pro-China Manasseh Sogavare — it is now etched in ink, with the new treaty declaring it will never allow a foreign military base on its soil.
For Mr Kabutaulaka, there is no doubt the treaty was done to "counter China".
He said the treaty itself was not "mind-shattering"; it was more its "impacts".
"We are already beginning to see that, with the Chinese police leaving,"
he said.
He highlighted the money pledged for the Solomon Islands government's "flagship policy on free education" as one element that would be well-received locally.
Minister for Pacific Island Affairs Pat Conroy agreed.
"One-third of Solomon Islands' children can't afford to enter the primary school system," he told the ABC.
"By supporting free education, this will transform the lives of hundreds of thousands of Solomon Islanders, and they will see the practical benefits of this very quickly.
"I'm confident that will add to the social licence of this treaty."
Whether that is understood in Solomon Islands is another matter.
'Sold its sovereignty'
"Solomon Islands has been for a number of years a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region. Those days are done, gone. We don't want to be there again," he said.
But in Solomon Islands you never say never. Politics is about as fluid as the Pacific Ocean that surrounds them.
As if on cue, the country's former leader and architect of China-Solomons security pact, Manasseh Sogavare, came out all guns blazing, declaring the country had "sold its sovereignty" to Australia.
Mr Sogavare, now the country's opposition leader, declared the treaty should be made public and tabled in parliament for debate.

The hypocrisy of this statement, coming from the man who refused to make public the China-Solomon Islands security deal, is not lost on the people who have watched this saga play out for the past four years (and for what it's worth, the Australian government has published the treaty in full and made a very big deal of it).
But either way, it goes to show that nothing is forever in the Pacific, and even more so in Solomon Islands.
And there is little doubt that inside that big, oversized sea container in Honiara called the Chinese embassy, they will be plotting, looking at ways to bite back.
